Reading · talent and practice

1.1 Discuss. Think of something you are good at. Were you born able to do it, or did you learn it? How long did it take?

KEY WORDS

deliberate practice planned, focused practice

an excuse a reason you give for not doing something

unwelcome not what you want to hear

an expert performer someone at the very top of a field

When Will I Be Famous?

Ask a class of eleven-year-olds what they want to be, and a surprising number will tell you they want to be famous. Not famous for anything in particular — just famous. Psychologists who study this find it depressing, but I'm not sure they should. What the children are describing isn't really fame. It is the feeling of being unusually good at something, which seems a perfectly reasonable thing to want.

The problem is what they believe about how you get there. In survey after survey, young people say that success comes from talent: either you can do it or you can't. Adults who have actually become good at something say almost the opposite. They talk about the years when they weren't able to do it at all, the teacher who wouldn't let them give up, and the extremely boring practice they somehow managed to keep going.

Anders Ericsson, who spent a career studying expert performers, put it bluntly: nobody has ever been found who reached the top of a difficult field without an enormous amount of deliberate practice. Talent may decide how quickly you improve at the beginning. It appears to decide remarkably little after that.

This ought to be encouraging news, and for some students it is. For others it is unwelcome, because it takes away the excuse. If you can't play the piano, you are not someone born unable to play the piano; you are someone who hasn't practised. That is harder to hear — and far more useful.

2

Grammar · modals and phrases of ability

PRESENTATION

PRESENT ability — can / can't · be able to · be good at + -ing:

I can swim. · She's able to work in three languages. · He's good at explaining things.

PAST ability — could / couldn't for general ability; was/were able to or managed to for one occasion:

I could read at four. · The fire was bad, but everyone was able to get out.

OTHER TENSES — can has no infinitive or future, so use be able to:

I'll be able to drive next year. · I've never been able to sing.

General ability — could

One occasion — was able to / managed to

I could swim when I was five.

I was able to swim to the boat that day.

She could play the violin at six.

She managed to play the piece perfectly.

He couldn't cook at all.

He didn't manage to book a table.

We could all speak some Russian.

We were able to explain the problem.

ERROR WARNING

can has no infinitive and no future form — use be able to:

I want to can drive. ✗ I want to be able to drive. ✓

I will can help you. ✗ I'll be able to help you. ✓

For one successful action in the past, use was/were able to or managed to, not could:

I could pass the exam last week. ✗ I managed to pass the exam last week. ✓

4

Everyday English · offering and asking for help

4.1 Read the conversation.

Aziza You're good with computers, aren't you?

Jasur Reasonably. Why — what's the problem?

Aziza I can't get this file to open. Could you have a look?

Jasur Of course. Do you want me to try it on my laptop?

Aziza Would you? That'd be great.

Jasur No problem at all. It won't take long, will it?

Aziza I hope not. Thanks — I really appreciate it.

Asking for help

Offering help

Accepting and thanking

Could you have a look at…?

Do you want me to…?

Would you? That'd be great.

Would you mind + -ing?

Shall I…?

Thanks — I appreciate it.

Is there any chance you could…?

Let me… / I'll do it.

That's really kind of you.

ERROR WARNING

Question tags: a positive sentence takes a negative tag, and the reverse:

You're good with computers, aren't you? · It won't take long, will it?

You are good with computers, isn't it? ✗ · Would you mind takes -ing: Would you mind helping me?
